contents.html: Smart home technologies may expose adopters to increased risk to network security, information privacy, and physical safety. However, users may lack understanding of the privacy and security implications, while devices fail to provide transparency and configuration options. This results in little meaningful mitigation action to protect users’ security and privacy. To better understand users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security, we conducted an in-depth interview study of 40 smart home users. In this document, we report the study findings related to perceptions of data collection/use, privacy and security concerns, and mitigations employed to alleviate concerns. We found that users have varied, and often unclear, understandings of how smart home data are collected and used. In addition, although users may have security and privacy concerns, many participants displayed a willingness to accept risks in favor of smart home benefits, and they feel limited responsibility for mitigating these due to constrained options or lack of knowledge to enact more sophisticated countermeasures. While this report is not meant to be prescriptive, an understanding of user perceptions may be used to inform future smart home security and privacy guidance for manufacturers and users.
contents.html_ja: スマートホーム技術は、導入者をネットワークセキュリティ、情報プライバシー、身体的安全に関するリスクの増大にさらす場合があります。しかし、デバイスが透明性や設定オプションを提供しない一方で、ユーザーはプライバシーとセキュリティへの影響を理解していない場合があります。その結果、ユーザーのセキュリティとプライバシーを守るための有意義なリスク緩和策はほとんど講じられていません。スマートホームのプライバシーとセキュリティに対するユーザーの認識をよりよく理解するため、スマートホームユーザー40人を対象に詳細なインタビュー調査を実施しました。本書では、データの収集・利用に対する認識、プライバシーとセキュリティへの懸念、懸念を軽減するために用いられている緩和策に関する調査結果を報告します。調査の結果、ユーザーはスマートホームのデータがどのように収集・利用されるかについて、さまざまな理解を持ち、その理解は多くの場合不明確であることがわかりました。さらに、ユーザーはセキュリティとプライバシーへの懸念を抱いている場合があるものの、多くの参加者はスマートホームの利点を優先してリスクを受け入れる意向を示しました。また、選択肢が限られていることや、より高度な対策を講じる知識が不足していることから、それらのリスクを緩和する責任は自分たちにはあまりないと感じています。本報告書は規範を示すことを意図したものではありませんが、ユーザーの認識を理解することで、製造者とユーザーに向けた今後のスマートホームのセキュリティおよびプライバシーのガイダンス策定に役立てることができます。

contents.html: The Internet of Things (IoT) market is rapidly expanding, with the number of IoT devices expected to increase from 26 billion in 2019 to 75 billion in 2025 [1]. With this increase, IoT smart home technology is becoming more pervasive, with an annual growth of 31% [2] and 34% of broadband households forecasted to have smart home systems by 2025 [3]. While early adopters of smart home technology have typically been more technically savvy, smart home devices are increasingly being purchased by users who may not understand the technology’s privacy and security implications [2]. Within the current dynamic threat and technology environment, the uptick of smart home technology adoption may expose users to increased risks to their network security, privacy of their information, and quite possibly their physical safety [4, 5]. As such, it is imperative that smart home consumers be able to protect the security and privacy of their devices while still being able to enjoy the benefits of the technology.
contents.html_ja: モノのインターネット（IoT）市場は急速に拡大しており、IoT デバイスの数は 2019年の 260 億台から 2025年には 750 億台に増加すると予想されています [1]。この増加に伴い、IoT のスマートホーム技術はますます普及しており、年間成長率は 31% [2] で、2025年までにブロードバンド世帯の 34% がスマートホームシステムを持つと予測されています [3]。スマートホーム技術の初期の導入者は、一般に技術に詳しい人が多かったのに対し、スマートホームデバイスは、その技術がプライバシーとセキュリティにもたらす影響を理解していない可能性のあるユーザーによって、ますます購入されるようになっています [2]。現在の動的な脅威と技術の環境において、スマートホーム技術の導入の増加は、ユーザーを、ネットワークセキュリティ、情報のプライバシー、そしておそらくは身体的安全に対するリスクの増大にさらす可能性があります [4, 5]。そのため、スマートホームの消費者が、その技術の利点を享受し続けながら、デバイスのセキュリティとプライバシーを守れるようにすることが不可欠です。

contents.html_ja: しかし、スマートホームデバイスは、プライバシーとセキュリティの保護や設定オプションの透明性を提供していない場合があります。これは、セキュリティを機能性よりも二の次と見なしている製造者がいるためかもしれません [6]。また、プライバシーは、データの収益化という製造者のビジネスモデルと直接衝突する可能性があるため、既存の制御を分かりにくくしつつ、自らを法的な責任追及から守ることが、製造者の利益にかなう場合があります。これに、ユーザーがスマートホームデバイスの技術、機能、プライバシー、セキュリティについて深く理解していないことが重なって、消費者のセキュリティとプライバシーを守るための意味のある緩和策がほとんど取られていない可能性があります [7–10]。
contents.html: However, smart home devices may fail to provide transparency of privacy and security protections and configuration options, perhaps because some manufacturers view security as secondary to functionality [6]. Also, privacy may directly conflict with manufacturers’ business models of data monetization, so it may be in their interest to obfuscate existing controls while protecting themselves from legal repercussions. In combination with users’ lack of in-depth understanding of smart home device technology, functionalities, and privacy and security, there may be little meaningful mitigation actions being taken to protect consumer security and privacy [7–10].

contents.html: To improve this situation, manufacturers and third parties with influence in the smart home space can follow a user-centered approach [11]. This approach requires empirical evidence of end users’ perceptions, needs, wants, and challenges in order to create meaningful and effective privacy and security controls, interfaces, guidelines, and other resources to support users. It is also important to understand what actions users are willing and able to take on their own versus which functions they feel are the duty of or would be better suited to others.

contents.html: The results revealed perceptions of data collection and use, privacy and security concerns, and mitigations employed to alleviate concerns. We found that users have varied, and often unclear, understandings of how smart home data are collected and used. In addition, although users may have security and privacy concerns, many participants displayed a willingness to accept risks in favor of smart home benefits, and they feel limited responsibility for mitigating these due to constrained options or lack of knowledge to enact more sophisticated countermeasures. This NISTIR is meant to report user-centric research findings that may help to inform smart home security and privacy guidance for manufacturers and users. However, we do not explicitly prescribe guidance or recommendations in this document.

contents.html: Data analysis started with coding, which involves categorization of data. In the case of interview data, units of text are labeled based on their topic, with these labels being called “codes.” Units may consist of a phrase, sentence, or multiple sentences. For example, the unit of text “the companies that have the information, you know data breaches happen. . . So that was a concern as well” was assigned the code “Data Breach Concerns.” We employed both deductive and inductive coding practices, which allowed for an emergence of themes. Deductive coding involves starting with pre-defined codes that the researchers believe will appear in the data. With inductive coding, codes emerge from the data itself.
contents.html_ja: データ分析は、データの分類を伴うコーディングから始まりました。インタビューデータの場合、テキストの単位がトピックに基づいてラベル付けされ、これらのラベルは「コード」と呼ばれます。単位は、語句、1 文、または複数の文で構成されることがあります。たとえば、「その情報を持っている企業、ほら、データ侵害は起きますよね。…だからそれも懸念でした」というテキストの単位には、「データ侵害への懸念」というコードが割り当てられました。私たちは、演繹的なコーディングと帰納的なコーディングの両方を用い、これによりテーマが浮かび上がるようにしました。演繹的コーディングでは、研究者がデータに現れると考える、あらかじめ定義されたコードから始めます。帰納的コーディングでは、コードはデータそのものから現れます。

contents.html_ja: インタビューの文字起こしの分析は、研究課題に基づく事前のコードリストの作成から始まりました。最初のコードリストを使い、研究チームの 3 人のメンバーがそれぞれ個別に 4 件のインタビューの一部をコーディングし、その後グループとして集まり、コードの適用について議論しました。関連するコードは、軸足コードと呼ばれる上位のカテゴリにグループ化されました。たとえば、「データ侵害への懸念」「音声／映像へのアクセス」「金銭的損失」というコードは、「セキュリティ上の懸念」という軸足コードにまとめられました。最終的なコードブック（分析に使用するコードのリスト）の一部として、すべてのコードが「操作的に定義」されました。これは、すべてのコーダー間で理解が一致するよう、各コードを正式に定義することを伴います。
contents.html: Analysis of the interview transcripts began with the development of an a priori code list based on the research questions. Using the initial code list, each of the three research team members individually coded a subset of four interviews, then met as a group to discuss code application. Related codes were grouped into higher-level categories, called axial codes. For example, the codes “Data Breach Concerns,” “Audio/video access,” and “Financial loss” were combined into an axial code called “Security Concerns.” As part of the final codebook (a list of codes to be used in analysis), all codes were “operationalized,” which involves formally defining each code to ensure understanding among all coders.

contents.html_ja: 次に、コードブックを使って、残りのインタビューを独立してコーディングし、各文字起こしは 2 人の研究者がコーディングしました。その後、各コーダーのペアが、コードの適用の違いを確認し、解決しました。分析フェーズを通じて、定期的なグループ会議の中で、コード間の関係と私たちの解釈について議論しました。
contents.html: Using the codebook, we then coded the remaining interviews independently, with each transcript coded by two researchers. Each pair of coders then examined and resolved differences in code application. Throughout the analysis phase, during regular group meetings, we discussed relationships among the codes and our interpretations.

contents.html: 2.4 Limitations
contents.html_ja: 2.4 制約事項
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.12の節見出し

contents.html: As with any interview study, participant responses are subject to recall, self-report, and social desirability biases. In addition, the participants, who were generally highly educated professionals in a high-income metropolitan area, may not be fully representative of the overall smart home user population in the U.S. However, our study population appears to mirror smart home adopters characterized in prior industry surveys [15]. We also acknowledge that U.S. smart home users may have different privacy and security attitudes from those in other countries, for example, due to political or cultural factors related to privacy expectations and tolerance. In addition, our study only captures perceptions of smart home adopters of multiple devices, so does not adequately capture those of limited adopters or non-adopters. These limitations could be addressed with replication of this study in other countries or a global quantitative survey informed by the results of our study. However, even with its limitations, the study serves as an exploratory investigation that can inform subsequent surveys of broader populations.
contents.html_ja: どのインタビュー調査でもそうであるように、参加者の回答は、想起バイアス、自己報告バイアス、社会的望ましさバイアスの影響を受けます。加えて、参加者は、高所得の大都市圏に住む、一般に高学歴の専門職であり、米国のスマートホームユーザー全体を十分に代表していない可能性があります。ただし、私たちの調査対象者は、過去の業界調査 [15] で特徴づけられたスマートホームの導入者を反映しているように見えます。また、米国のスマートホームユーザーは、たとえばプライバシーへの期待や許容度に関する政治的・文化的要因のために、他の国のユーザーとは異なるプライバシーとセキュリティへの態度を持っている可能性があることも認識しています。さらに、本調査は、複数のデバイスを導入しているスマートホーム導入者の認識しか捉えておらず、導入が限定的な人や非導入者の認識は十分に捉えていません。これらの制約は、他の国での本調査の再現、または本調査の結果を踏まえた世界規模の定量調査によって対処できます。しかし、制約があっても、本調査は、より広い母集団を対象とするその後の調査に情報を提供できる探索的な調査として役立ちます。

contents.html: We asked participants where they thought collected data go. Twenty-three participants thought that data are sent to the smart home manufacturer. Eight of these made specific mention of the manufacturer’s cloud or cloud service as a destination. For example, one participant said, “Devices that are collecting sensor information, all that sensor information leaves your house and is stored in a cloud service” (P11_A). Others referred to manufacturer servers or databases: “it goes to the companies, I guess their servers, a database” (P28_A).

contents.html: Participants were asked how they think the data collected by smart home devices are used. Several believed that data are analyzed by manufacturers for product improvement purposes. From a functionality perspective, one participant commented that his smart vacuum cleaner “was sending back maps of the area that it’s cleaning and scoping out, so it can improve and build better maps” (P13_A). Another remarked, “I’m sure they’re also collecting information about the device, if it’s faulty or if you know maybe how quickly their customer support team reaches out to us” (P28_A). Data analysis was also viewed as a way to improve future versions of the product or inform the design of completely new products. A participant believed that, through data collection, manufacturers “study consumers’ habits, the behavior, so that will help them to come up with better products to solve their needs” (P36_A). An owner of a smart thermostat viewed the data as contributing to a larger effort to save energy: “it definitely goes into a database where they collect and analyze that information which actually, I’m okay with. If it’s going to save the environment, sure” (P6_U).
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、スマートホームデバイスが収集したデータがどのように利用されると思うかを尋ねられました。何人かは、データが製品改良のために製造者によって分析されると考えていました。機能性の観点から、ある参加者は、自分のスマート掃除機が「掃除している範囲と探索している範囲の地図を送り返していて、それによって改良し、よりよい地図を作れるようになる」とコメントしました（P13_A）。別の参加者は、「デバイスについての情報、たとえば故障しているかどうかや、カスタマーサポートチームがどれくらい早くこちらに連絡してくるかなども収集しているのは確かでしょう」と述べました（P28_A）。データ分析は、製品の将来のバージョンの改良や、まったく新しい製品の設計に情報を提供する手段とも見なされていました。ある参加者は、データ収集を通じて製造者が「消費者の習慣や行動を研究し、それがニーズを満たすよりよい製品を考え出す助けになる」と考えていました（P36_A）。スマートサーモスタットの所有者は、データを、省エネというより大きな取り組みに貢献するものと見ていました。「情報を収集して分析するデータベースに確実に入っていますが、実はそれは構いません。環境を守ることになるなら、もちろんです」（P6_U）。

contents.html_ja: データの送信先に関する参加者の回答にも表れているように、インタビューを受けたスマートホームユーザーの多くは、データが製造者やサードパーティによってターゲット広告に利用されると考えていました。ある参加者は、製造者は「データマイニングをしています。…悪意はないと思います。つまり、それに関することはすべて製品を売るためで、インターネットに関することはすべて製品を売るためです」と述べました（P40_A）。別の参加者は、製造者やサードパーティが「その情報を入手して、あなたの居住地や家にどんな種類のデバイスがあるかを知っているので、広告付きのメールをあなたを対象に送る可能性がある」と考えていました（P11_A）。あるユーザーは、データが「市場で何が人気かを把握するために、こうした調査を行う機関に」売られていると話しました（P21_U）。
contents.html: As also reflected in participant responses related to data destination, many of the interviewed smart home users thought that data are used by the manufacturer or third parties for targeted advertising. One participant said that manufacturers are “doing data mining. . . It’s not malicious I don’t think. I mean everything about it is to sell you a product, everything about the internet is to sell you a product” (P40_A). Another thought that manufacturers or third parties “take that information and potentially target emails with advertisements to you, because they know where you live, they might know what type of devices you have in your house” (P11_A). A user talked about data being sold “to agencies that do these surveys to kind of figure out what’s popular out there in the market” (P21_U).

contents.html: In the first half of interviews, participants were asked if they had any hesitations prior to device purchase, if they had any general concerns about their smart home devices, and what other members of the household thought about the devices. Two-thirds of participants mentioned privacy-related concerns and half acknowledged security concerns in the context of these questions. These unprompted mentions offer interesting insight into whether privacy and security concerns are in the forefront of users’ minds.
contents.html_ja: インタビューの前半では、参加者は、デバイスの購入前にためらいがあったか、自分のスマートホームデバイスについて一般的な懸念があるか、世帯の他のメンバーがそのデバイスをどう考えていたかを尋ねられました。これらの質問の文脈で、参加者の 3 分の 2 がプライバシーに関する懸念に言及し、半数がセキュリティ上の懸念を認めました。こうした自発的な言及は、プライバシーとセキュリティへの懸念がユーザーの意識の前面にあるかどうかについて、興味深い知見を与えます。

contents.html_ja: その後、参加者は、プライバシーとセキュリティへの懸念について明示的に尋ねられました。プライバシーまたはセキュリティについて個人的に懸念している参加者もいましたが、その程度はさまざまでした。また、他者（例: 家族、友人、メディア）が表明した懸念に言及したものの、自分自身は抱いていない参加者もいました。たとえば、ある参加者は、自分とパートナーとの間でのプライバシーに関する懸念の違いに言及しました。「[バーチャルアシスタント]について、私はためらいはありませんでした。婚約者はためらいました。常に聞かれているのが好きではないからです」（P10_A）。
contents.html: Participants were later explicitly asked about their privacy and security concerns. In some cases, participants were personally concerned about privacy or security but to varying degrees. Other participants mentioned concerns that were expressed by others (e.g., family members, friends, media) but not personally held. For example, one participant mentioned a disparity in privacy concerns between him and his partner: “The [virtual assistant], I didn’t have any hesitations. My fiancé did because she doesn’t like being listened to all the time” (P10_A).

contents.html: Several participants expressed concerns that their personal financial information could be obtained should their smart home devices be hacked (security context) or if their information be divulged (privacy). Some of this concern stemmed from payment and contact information stored as part of an account for a smart home app or service. For example, one participant commented, “while I don’t care what people see on my [smart entertainment device], I would care if they see my credit card information” (P37_A). A smart home device administrator put financial concerns above other types of privacy:

contents.html: One of the concerns mentioned in the privacy context was the profiling of household members, including their pattern of life, what kinds of things they like, approximate ages of household members, and “the literal movements of our family,. . . the times that we’re there and the times that we’re not, and who’s there” (P1_A). Profiling could be accomplished by looking at individual pieces of data collected by smart home devices but most often when examined in aggregate, as discussed by one participant:
contents.html_ja: プライバシーの文脈で挙げられた懸念の 1 つは、世帯のメンバーのプロファイリングで、生活パターン、好きなものの種類、世帯メンバーのおおよその年齢、そして「家族の文字どおりの動き、…私たちがいる時間といない時間、誰がいるか」が含まれます（P1_A）。プロファイリングは、スマートホームデバイスが収集した個々のデータを見ることでも可能ですが、ある参加者が論じたように、集約して調べた場合が最も多くなります:

contents.html_ja: 「彼らが記録する情報は、通常はデバイスがどのように使われているかについてのものですが、間接的に何かを推測できるのは確かです。そして、すべてのデバイスのデータにアクセスできれば、私の日々の習慣の全体像をおそらく組み立てられます」（P15_A）。

contents.html_ja: 3.2.6 データの販売とターゲット広告
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.22の項見出し

contents.html: Also within the privacy context, many consumers suspect that the data collected by their smart home devices is being used for targeted ads, either by the manufacturer or by other companies that buy the data. As one participant remarked, “All these companies, they’re mining our data. They’re trying to see what they can eventually sell us, or sell our information to somebody” (P28_A). While some participants were not bothered by this, others were. One smart home owner commented, “I hate targeted ads. I hate them with a passion” (P17_A). Another expressed his discomfort with a perceived correlation about commands his family gives to their virtual assistant and ads they see on other online platforms:
contents.html_ja: これもプライバシーの文脈ですが、多くの消費者は、自分のスマートホームデバイスが収集したデータが、製造者や、データを購入する他の企業によってターゲット広告に使われているのではないかと疑っています。ある参加者が述べたように、「これらの企業はみな、私たちのデータをマイニングしています。最終的に私たちに何を売れるか、あるいは私たちの情報を誰かに売れるかを見極めようとしているのです」（P28_A）。これを気にしない参加者もいましたが、気にする参加者もいました。あるスマートホームの所有者は、「ターゲット広告が嫌いです。心の底から嫌いです」とコメントしました（P17_A）。別の参加者は、家族がバーチャルアシスタントに出すコマンドと、他のオンラインプラットフォームで見る広告との間に相関があるように感じられることに対する不快感を表明しました:
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.22と照合し一致

contents.html: “The amount of times we’ve said a word and all of a sudden seen ads for things is way too high to be not a thing, so that kind of weirds me out. . . I think most of these companies are a little too hungry for ad info, and so they just take anything and everything, regardless of how creepy it can be. Sometimes it’s a little too personal” (P29_A).
contents.html_ja: 「ある言葉を口にしたら突然、それに関する広告が表示される回数が多すぎて、偶然とは思えないので、ちょっと気味が悪いです。…これらの企業の大半は、広告情報に少し貪欲すぎて、どんなに気味が悪くても、何でもかんでも取っていくのだと思います。ときどき、少し個人的すぎます」（P29_A）。

contents.html: 3.2.7 Unknowns of Data Collection
contents.html_ja: 3.2.7 データ収集に関する不明点

contents.html: About 40% of participants were concerned that they did not have a good grasp on smart home device data collection and usage, which led to privacy concerns. One participant commented, “You have no idea when it’s communicating to the manufacturer or what it’s communicating to the manufacturer. And I think the privacy aspects of that are underappreciated” (P13_A). A smart home do-it-yourselfer discussed challenges finding ground truth about data collection:
contents.html_ja: 約 40% の参加者は、スマートホームデバイスのデータ収集と利用を十分に把握していないことを懸念しており、それがプライバシーへの懸念につながっていました。ある参加者は、「デバイスがいつ製造者と通信しているのか、製造者に何を通信しているのか、まったくわかりません。そして、その点のプライバシーの側面は、過小評価されていると思います」とコメントしました（P13_A）。ある自作愛好のスマートホームユーザーは、データ収集に関する実態を把握することの難しさについて論じました:
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23と照合し一致

contents.html: “Unless you really monitor what’s going out of your network, you really don’t know what the devices are broadcasting. There’s really no firewall that is looking at whether the devices are broadcasting what they’re supposed to. For instance, is your [virtual assistant] device, is that actually listening to more than what you would expect it to? Is it relaying information out? Same with a video camera,. . . doorbell, whatever type of device. Is it doing more than you think? Are there functions inside of these devices that are not advertised, but capable of doing things?” (P11_A).
contents.html_ja: 「ネットワークから出ていくものを本気で監視しない限り、デバイスが何を送信しているのかは本当にわかりません。デバイスが送信すべきものを送信しているかを見るファイアウォールは、実質的にありません。たとえば、[バーチャルアシスタント]デバイスは、実際に期待以上のことを聞いていませんか。情報を外に中継していませんか。ビデオカメラ、…ドアベル、どんな種類のデバイスでも同じです。考えている以上のことをしていませんか。これらのデバイスの中に、宣伝されていないけれど何かを実行できる機能がないか」（P11_A）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23と照合し一致

contents.html: One smart home device owner lamented that privacy policies and user level agreements are typically not transparent about data collection: “You don’t really know what they’re collecting because they can use language to mislead you. It’s legal, but misleading” (P31_A).
contents.html_ja: あるスマートホームデバイスの所有者は、プライバシーポリシーやユーザー向け契約が、通常はデータ収集について透明ではないと嘆きました。「彼らが何を収集しているのか、本当にはわかりません。言葉づかいで誤解させることができるからです。合法ですが、誤解を招きます」（P31_A）。

contents.html: 3.2.8 Device Hacking
contents.html_ja: 3.2.8 デバイスのハッキング
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23の項見出し

contents.html: Within the security context, participants mentioned that they were concerned about their devices being hacked by unauthorized or malicious actors, as expressed by one participant who worried that hackers would be able to “shut off, or dismantle, or mess with the system that I have in place” (P37_A). In fact, the threat of device exploitation underpinned many of the privacy and security concerns discovered in our study. For example, exploitation could lead to unauthorized individuals gaining access to audio and video feeds. Governments could hack into devices or their companion apps for surveillance purposes.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティの文脈では、参加者は、権限のない者や悪意ある攻撃者によるデバイスのハッキングを懸念していると述べました。ある参加者は、ハッカーが「自分が設置したシステムを停止したり、分解したり、いじったりできる」ことを心配していました（P37_A）。実際、デバイスの悪用の脅威は、本調査で明らかになったプライバシーとセキュリティへの懸念の多くの根底にありました。たとえば、悪用によって、権限のない個人が音声や映像のフィードにアクセスできるようになる可能性があります。政府が監視の目的でデバイスやそのコンパニオンアプリに侵入する可能性もあります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23の2段落に分け、合字を直す

contents.html_ja: 何人かは、自分のスマートホームデバイスがハッキングされることの容易さの可能性と、避けられないという認識について論じました。ある参加者はこう述べました:
contents.html: Several discussed the potential ease and perceived inevitability of their smart home devices being hacked. One remarked:
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23の2段落に分け、合字を直す

contents.html: “It’s as simple as username and passwords. . . All these apps also have a back end where you can go and pull it up on the Internet. For example, I go to [website] to pull up my cameras. . . If you just stole my username and password, again, you have the same access” (P8_A).
contents.html_ja: 「ユーザー名とパスワードだけの簡単なことです。…これらのアプリにはどれも、インターネット上で呼び出せるバックエンドがあります。たとえば、私は[ウェブサイト]にアクセスして、自分のカメラを呼び出します。…私のユーザー名とパスワードを盗めば、やはり同じアクセスが得られます」（P8_A）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23と照合し一致

contents.html: Another was pessimistic about having any sense of security:
contents.html_ja: 別の参加者は、セキュリティの感覚を持つことに悲観的でした:
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23と照合し一致

contents.html: “I would not entrust my security in any way to any of these devices to be honest. It may not be the fault of the device itself. Any type of connectivity that you have to the internet is hackable, and if it’s not, tomorrow it will be. If they haven’t figured how to break through some firewall, somebody will (P40_A).
contents.html_ja: 「正直なところ、私は自分のセキュリティを、これらのデバイスのどれにも一切委ねません。デバイス自体の落ち度ではないかもしれません。インターネットに接続するあらゆる種類の接続はハッキング可能であり、そうでなければ明日にはそうなります。ファイアウォールを突破する方法をまだ誰も見つけていなくても、誰かが見つけます」（P40_A）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.23と照合し一致

contents.html: One participant was concerned about smart home vulnerabilities in certain types of devices based on conversations he had with colleagues in which he learned “each manufacturer is actually just borrowing security APIs instead of creating their own, and the APIs specifically have holes in them. So the same vulnerability is being propagated across vendors” (P13_A). Others were concerned based on their exposure to news stories about smart home devices being compromised. For P34_A, one such story prompted him to be more suspicious of his devices:
contents.html_ja: ある参加者は、同僚との会話から、「各製造者は実際には自社でセキュリティ API を作るのではなく、セキュリティ API を借りているだけで、その API には特に穴があります。そのため、同じ脆弱性がベンダー間で広がっている」ことを知り、特定の種類のデバイスにおけるスマートホームの脆弱性を懸念していました（P13_A）。スマートホームデバイスが危殆化されたというニュース記事に触れたことを理由に懸念する人もいました。P34_A の場合、そのような記事の 1 つがきっかけとなり、自分のデバイスをより疑うようになりました:

contents.html: “There was just an article I read about all the smart devices and now how they stole people’s information. And, I’m a little hesitant. So with my security camera,. . . sometimes I feel, you know it takes pictures without my consent. And I feel some information is going somewhere that I have no control over” (P34_A).
contents.html_ja: 「すべてのスマートデバイスと、今や人々の情報がどのように盗まれたかについての記事を読んだばかりです。それで、少しためらっています。だから、セキュリティカメラについても、…ときどき、同意なしに写真を撮っているように感じます。そして、自分には制御できないどこかに、何らかの情報が行っているように感じます」（P34_A）。

contents.html: 3.2.9 Physical Safety
contents.html_ja: 3.2.9 身体的安全
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.24の項見出し

contents.html: Participants believed that security vulnerabilities and device hacking could also result in safety consequences since smart home devices often have the ability to make changes to the physical environment. For example, since many of the participants owned smart thermostats, there were concerns about hackers being able to control the heating and air in the house, which could impact the physical well-being of household members. One smart home user wondered, “what if someone hacks into our phones and. . . with the [smart thermostat] they try to change the temperature if we’ve already set it and they go in and they try to reconfigure it on their own?” (P12_U).
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、スマートホームデバイスには物理的な環境を変更できる能力が備わっていることが多いため、セキュリティ上の脆弱性やデバイスのハッキングが、安全性に関わる結果をもたらす可能性もあると考えていました。たとえば、多くの参加者がスマートサーモスタットを所有していたため、ハッカーが家の暖房や空調を制御できるようになり、世帯メンバーの身体的な健康に影響を及ぼす可能性があるという懸念がありました。あるスマートホームユーザーは、「誰かが私たちのスマートフォンに侵入して、…[スマートサーモスタット]で、すでに設定してある温度を勝手に変更しようとしたら、どうなるのだろう」と疑問に思っていました（P12_U）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.24の2段落に分け、行末ハイフンを直す

contents.html_ja: また、誤作動したデバイスやハッキングされたデバイスにより、スマートアラームシステムやセキュリティカメラが無効にされた場合、侵入者が家に入りやすくなる可能性を懸念する参加者もいました。スマートドアロックを持つユーザーは、「誰かが私たちのシステムをハッキングできたら、玄関のドアを簡単に開けられてしまいます」と述べました（P14_U）。P31_A は、「犯罪者が十分に賢ければ、無線を無効にして、これらの家に入るでしょう」とコメントしました。別の参加者は、スマートガレージドアオープナーが悪用された場合に考えられる危険について話しました:
contents.html: Others were concerned that malfunctioning or hacked devices could allow intruders easier access to the home should smart alarm systems or security cameras be disabled. A user with a smart door lock said, “If somebody could hack our system, they could easily open our front door” (P14_U). P31_A commented, “If criminals were wise enough, they’d just knock out the wireless and enter these homes.” Another participant talked about potential dangers if his smart garage door opener was exploited:
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.24の2段落に分け、行末ハイフンを直す

contents.html: “I would say that it actually could be detrimental to my safety because who knows if it’s hackable and they can get into my house. I just gave you the entryway. So, you don’t need to pick a lock at all. You just got to get into my Wi-Fi” (P8_A).
contents.html_ja: 「それは実際に、私の安全に有害になり得ると言えます。ハッキングできて家に入れるかどうか、誰にもわからないからです。今、侵入経路をお話ししました。だから、鍵をこじ開ける必要はまったくありません。私の Wi-Fi に入り込みさえすればいいのです」（P8_A）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.24と照合し一致

contents.html: Related to the household profiling concern, information collected by smart home devices, if accessed by unauthorized individuals, could provide insight into when a home is or is not occupied, thus facilitating the timing of home invasions. One participant remarked, “If somebody is. . . actually able to associate when you’re home and when you’re not home based on the sensors and other things you have in your house, they could potentially target you” (P11_A). Another said:
contents.html_ja: 世帯のプロファイリングへの懸念に関連して、スマートホームデバイスが収集した情報に権限のない個人がアクセスすると、家に人がいる時間といない時間がわかるため、押し入りのタイミングを容易にする可能性があります。ある参加者は、「誰かが、…家にあるセンサーなどに基づいて、あなたが家にいるときといないときを実際に関連付けられるなら、あなたを標的にできる可能性があります」と述べました（P11_A）。別の参加者はこう述べました:

So, you know, if you can get into the system and say, it’s set to 78 [degrees Fahrenheit] until 5:00, and then it goes down to 72” (P18_A).

contents.html: 3.2.10 Other Security Concerns
contents.html_ja: 3.2.10 その他のセキュリティ上の懸念
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.25の項見出し

contents.html: Three other security-specific concerns were revealed during the interviews. Several participants were concerned about unauthorized individuals gaining access to the Wi-Fi network and other devices on that network through smart home devices, as noted by a participant: “I use my phone for everything, and it’s connected to my Wi-Fi. My Wi-Fi’s connected to my smart home. So I’m not a hacker, but I’m sure they find ways” (P41_U).
contents.html_ja: インタビューでは、セキュリティに特有の懸念がほかに 3 つ明らかになりました。何人かの参加者は、権限のない個人がスマートホームデバイスを通じて Wi-Fi ネットワークやそのネットワーク上の他のデバイスにアクセスすることを懸念しており、ある参加者はこう述べました。「私は何をするにもスマートフォンを使っていて、それは Wi-Fi に接続されています。私の Wi-Fi はスマートホームにつながっています。私はハッカーではありませんが、彼らは方法を見つけるはずです」（P41_U）。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.25の4段落に分け、行末ハイフンと合字を直す

contents.html_ja: 4 人は、スマートホームデバイスのアプリを悪用することで、メールやソーシャルメディアのアカウントなど、リンクされた他のアカウントにアクセスできてしまう可能性を心配していました。特に、アカウント間でパスワードが共通である場合です。たとえば、ある参加者は、「私たちの[アプリ]のアカウントはメールアドレスに関連付けられています。だから、それにハッキングすれば、私のメールアドレスが手に入り、そのメールからほかのあらゆるものにアクセスできます」と述べました（P30_U）。
contents.html: Four people were worried that access to other linked accounts, e.g., email and social media accounts, could be gained by exploiting smart home device apps, especially if passwords were common across accounts. For example, one participant said, “Our [app] account is associated with an email. So if you were to hack into it, you have my email and then from my email you can get anything else” (P30_U).
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.25の4段落に分け、行末ハイフンと合字を直す

contents.html_ja: 2 人の参加者は、デバイスの初期設定のセキュリティが不十分であることへの懸念に言及しました。1 人は、「これらのデバイスで懸念される点の 1 つは、初期状態で設定されているパスワードが、インターネットで簡単に調べられ、見つかってしまうことです」とコメントしました（P15_A）。
contents.html: Two participants mentioned a concern with devices having poor default security settings. One commented, “One of the areas of concern with these would be if they have default passwords out of the box that are easily looked up, easily found on the internet” (P15_A).

contents.html: 3.2.11 Lack of Concern

contents.html: We also found examples of various levels of lack of concern, with seven participants having neither privacy nor security concerns. In 24 cases, participants did not value the information collected by smart home devices, believing they would not be a worthwhile target. For example, one participant remarked, “I feel like you’ve got people who are pretty talented with computers and can get this stuff. . . I’m of the mindset, have at it. We don’t do anything cool in my house, anyways” (P8_A).
contents.html_ja: さまざまな程度の懸念の欠如の例もあり、7 人の参加者はプライバシーにもセキュリティにも懸念を持っていませんでした。24 件の事例では、参加者は、スマートホームデバイスが収集した情報に価値を認めておらず、自分は狙う価値のある標的ではないと考えていました。たとえば、ある参加者は、「コンピュータにかなり長けた人たちがいて、これを入手できるのだと思います。…やればいい、という考えです。うちでは、とにかく大したことは何もしていませんから」と述べました（P8_A）。

contents.html_ja: 私たちはまた、プライバシーの諦め [9] の証拠も確認しました。これは、ユーザーが、自分のデータはすでに他の手段（例: ソーシャルメディア、過去のデータ侵害など）で公に入手可能になっており、自分にできることは何もないと考えているものです（8 人の参加者）。ある参加者は、「みんながすでにあなたの情報をすべて持っていないと思うなら、おかしいですよ」と述べて、この諦めを表明しました（P17_A）。
contents.html: We also identified evidence of privacy resignation [9] in which users believe that their data are already publicly available via other means (e.g., social media, prior data breaches, etc.), and that there is nothing they can do about it (8 participants). A participant expressed this resignation when she said, “If you don’t think people have all of your information already, you’re crazy” (P17_A).

contents.html: 3.2.12 Risk Acceptance
contents.html_ja: 3.2.12 リスクの受容
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.26の項見出し

contents.html: Although some participants had concerns, they ultimately made a conscious choice, described as “willful ignorance” by P1_A, to accept privacy and security risks in exchange for perceived benefits. One participant expressed this as “Does the good outweigh the bad? I made the decision that, yes” (P8_8). Purchase decision and continued use signaled that risks did not cross users’ privacy/security threshold [16]. For example, one participant believed that the government was monitoring his smart home information but felt “This is the risk you take by getting a smart home. . . You don’t like it, go off the grid” (P26_A). Another discussed the trade-offs of owning smart home devices: “I know that it’s collecting personal data,. . . and I know there’s the potential of a security leak, but yet, I like having the convenience of having those things” (P1_A).
contents.html_ja: 懸念を持つ参加者もいましたが、彼らは最終的に、P1_Aが「意図的な無知」と表現したように、認識された利点と引き換えにプライバシーとセキュリティのリスクを受け入れるという意識的な選択をしました。ある参加者は、「良い点は悪い点を上回るか。私は、上回ると判断しました」と表現しました（P8_8）。購入の決定と継続的な使用は、リスクがユーザーのプライバシー／セキュリティのしきい値を超えなかったことを示していました [16]。たとえば、ある参加者は、政府が自分のスマートホーム情報を監視していると考えていましたが、「これはスマートホームを持つことで負うリスクです。…嫌なら、世間とのつながりを断って暮らせばいい」と感じていました（P26_A）。別の参加者は、スマートホームデバイスを所有することのトレードオフについて話しました。「個人データが収集されていることは知っていますし、…セキュリティ侵害の可能性があることも知っていますが、それでも、そうしたデバイスを使う利便性が気に入っています」（P1_A）。

contents.html: We explored reasons why some participants do not take mitigative actions. Obviously, some were simply not concerned enough to put forth the effort to take any action. Others were not aware of available options or were not given options. For example, one smart home user commented, “I’ve been given very little methods to alleviate the concerns. Usually the description of the controls aren’t specific enough for me to alleviate my concerns” (P13_A). Another said, “I can only image what you can and can’t turn off. There’s probably some things. Whether or not that actually happens or the user just thinks that it’s turned off, I don’t know” (P2_A).

contents.html: 4. Conclusion
contents.html_ja: 4. 結論
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p.28の章見出し「4. Conclusion」

contents.html: Via in-depth, semi-structured interviews, we investigated users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security. Our results suggest that users often have incomplete knowledge of what smart home data are collected and how they are being used. Despite having privacy and security concerns, users often accept risks as a tradeoff for perceived benefits. We also found that concerns do not always result in taking mitigative action for a number of reasons, most centered on lack of available options, transparency, or knowledge.
contents.html_ja: 詳細な半構造化インタビューを通じて、私たちはスマートホームのプライバシーとセキュリティに対するユーザーの認識を調査しました。結果は、ユーザーが、どのようなスマートホームのデータが収集され、どのように利用されているかについて、不完全な知識しか持っていないことが多いことを示唆しています。プライバシーとセキュリティへの懸念があるにもかかわらず、ユーザーは、認識された利点とのトレードオフとして、リスクを受け入れることがよくあります。また、懸念が必ずしも緩和策の実施につながるわけではなく、その理由は多くの場合、利用可能なオプション、透明性、または知識の不足にあることもわかりました。

contents.html_ja: スマートホームのプライバシーとセキュリティに対するユーザーの認識を調べることで、多様なユーザーがスマートホームデバイスを守るための行動を取りやすくなり、デバイスを自宅に導入する際により安心できるようにする方法を検討する手掛かりが得られ始めます。そうした方法には、プライバシーとセキュリティの仕組みの使いやすさの改善や、製造者が自社製品で提供できるオプションが含まれる可能性があります。
contents.html: The examination of users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security can begin to inform possible ways in which a diverse range of users can be more empowered to take protective actions for their smart home devices and feel more comfortable when introducing these devices into their homes. These might include improvements in the usability of privacy and security mechanisms or options that manufacturers could provide in their products.

The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsi-bilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-eﬀective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

Smart home technologies may expose adopters to increased risk to network security, in-formation privacy, and physical safety. However, users may lack understanding of the privacy and security implications, while devices fail to provide transparency and configu-ration options. This results in little meaningful mitigation action to protect users’ security and privacy. To better understand users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security, we conducted an in-depth interview study of 40 smart home users. In this document, we report the study findings related to perceptions of data collection/use, privacy and security concerns, and mitigations employed to alleviate concerns. We found that users have var-ied, and often unclear, understandings of how smart home data are collected and used. In addition, although users may have security and privacy concerns, many participants dis-played a willingness to accept risks in favor of smart home benefits, and they feel limited responsibility for mitigating these due to constrained options or lack of knowledge to enact more sophisticated countermeasures. While this report is not meant to be prescriptive, an understanding of user perceptions may be used to inform future smart home security and privacy guidance for manufacturers and users.

The Internet of Things (IoT) market is rapidly expanding, with the number of IoT devices expected to increase from 26 billion in 2019 to 75 billion in 2025 [1]. With this increase, IoT smart home technology is becoming more pervasive, with an annual growth of 31% [2] and 34% of broadband households forecasted to have smart home systems by 2025 [3]. While early adopters of smart home technology have typically been more technically savvy, smart home devices are increasingly being purchased by users who may not understand the technology’s privacy and security implications [2]. Within the current dynamic threat and technology environment, the uptick of smart home technology adoption may expose users to increased risks to their network security, privacy of their information, and quite possibly their physical safety [4, 5]. As such, it is imperative that smart home consumers be able to protect the security and privacy of their devices while still being able to enjoy the benefits of the technology. However, smart home devices may fail to provide transparency of privacy and security protections and configuration options, perhaps because some manufacturers view security as secondary to functionality [6]. Also, privacy may directly conflict with manufacturers’ business models of data monetization, so it may be in their interest to obfuscate existing controls while protecting themselves from legal repercussions. In combination with users’ lack of in-depth understanding of smart home device technology, functionalities, and pri-vacy and security, there may be little meaningful mitigation actions being taken to protect consumer security and privacy [7–10]. To improve this situation, manufacturers and third parties with influence in the smart home space can follow a user-centered approach [11]. This approach requires empirical evidence of end users’ perceptions, needs, wants, and challenges in order to create mean-ingful and eﬀective privacy and security controls, interfaces, guidelines, and other resources to support users. It is also important to understand what actions users are willing and able to take on their own versus which functions they feel are the duty of or would be better suited to others. Between February and June 2019, a research team led by the Visualization and Usabil-ity Group within the Information Technology Laboratory of the National Institute of Stan-dards and Technology (NIST) conducted an exploratory, semi-structured interview study of 40 smart home users to understand their experiences with smart home devices and their perceptions of smart home privacy and security. We previously published research papers focused on smart home privacy and security mitigations [12], updates [13], and perceptions of responsibility [14]. Therefore, we do not go into detail about these topics in this report. Rather, we describe a subset of study results that address the following research questions (RQs):
RQ1: What are users’ perceptions concerning the collection and use of data captured by
RQ2: What are smart home users’ privacy and security concerns, if any?
RQ3: What mitigation actions, if any, do smart home users take to address their privacy

The results revealed perceptions of data collection and use, privacy and security con-cerns, and mitigations employed to alleviate concerns. We found that users have varied, and often unclear, understandings of how smart home data are collected and used. In addi-tion, although users may have security and privacy concerns, many participants displayed a willingness to accept risks in favor of smart home benefits, and they feel limited respon-sibility for mitigating these due to constrained options or lack of knowledge to enact more sophisticated countermeasures. This NISTIR is meant to report user-centric research find-ings that may help to inform smart home security and privacy guidance for manufacturers and users. However, we do not explicitly prescribe guidance or recommendations in this document. The target audience of this report consists of researchers, designers/manufacturers, ad-ministrators, policy makers, decision makers, and creators of privacy and security guidance who perform work related to smart home devices. Users of smart home devices may also be interested in the study results. Readers who are less interested in the research methodology may wish to proceed directly to section 3: Results.

Between February and June of 2019, we conducted a semi-structured interview study of 40 smart home users to understand their perceptions of and experiences with the devices. Semi-structured interviews follow an established interview protocol while allowing the in-terviewer to ask unanticipated follow-up questions to clarify or expand upon participant responses. The National Institute of Standards and Technology Research Protections Oﬃce re-viewed the protocol for this project (ITL-2018-0118) and determined it meets the criteria for “exempt human subjects research” as defined in 15 CFR 27, the Common Rule for the Protection of Human Subjects. Prior to data collection, participants were informed of the study purpose and how their data would be protected. Data were recorded without per-sonal identifiers (instead using generic identifiers such as P10_A) and not linked back to individuals.

2.1 Participant Recruitment Eligible participants were adult users (18+ years of age) of smart home devices. A con-sumer research company did most of the recruitment (33 general public participants), while we identified an additional seven government employees to interview. General public par-ticipants were compensated with a $75 prepaid card. All participants lived in the Maryland-Virginia-District of Columbia region of the U.S. To determine eligibility for the study, prospective participants first completed an on-line screening survey about their smart home devices, their role with the devices (decision maker, purchaser, installer, administrator, troubleshooter, user), professional background, basic demographic information (age, gender), and number of household members. After re-viewing the screening information, to ensure we found information-rich cases that covered the spectrum of smart home device users, we purposively selected participants for inter-views if they had multiple smart home devices for which they were an active user. Despite a review of the screening questionnaire, one interviewed participant (P5) was found not to have any smart home devices (only a smartphone), so was excluded from study analysis. For the purposes of the study, we defined smart home devices as being networked de-vices in the following categories:
Smart security: e.g., security cameras, motion detectors, door locks
Smart entertainment: e.g., smart televisions, speakers, streaming devices, other con-
Home environment: e.g., smart plugs, energy consumption monitors, lighting, thermostats,
Smart appliances: e.g., refrigerators, coﬀee pots, robot vacuums, washers
Virtual assistants: e.g., voice-controlled devices such as Amazon Echo (colloquially called

Participant demographics are shown in Table 1. Of the 40 participants, 32 had installed and administered the devices (indicated with an A after the participant ID), and eight were non-administrative users of the devices (indicated with a U). Twenty-two (55%) were male and 18 (45%) were female. The majority (70%) were between the ages of 30 and 49 (see Figure 1). Participants were highly educated with 18 (45%) having a master’s degree or above and another 20 (50%) with a BS/BA. Thirty-four participants lived in multi-person households, with four couples among the participants (interviewed individually). Figure 5 shows the general categories of smart home devices in participants’ homes. All but one participant had three or more individual smart home devices, with 34 (85%) having three or more diﬀerent types of devices.

In addition to the screening survey, we collected data via 40 in-person interviews. Inter-views lasted between 22 and 80 minutes, averaging 41 minutes. All interviews were audio recorded and transcribed. Prior to the interviews, the interview protocol was reviewed by an IoT domain expert to ensure the usage of correct terminology and consideration of reasonable aspects of smart home use. We also piloted the protocol with four individuals to determine face validity of the questions, appropriate use of language, and timing. The protocol was refined based on these inputs.

original_blocks.html: Interview questions addressed several areas in the following order: understanding of smart home terminology; purchase decision process; general use; general concerns, likes, and dislikes; installation and troubleshooting; privacy and data collection/use; security; and safety. In this paper, we focus only on collected data pertaining to privacy and security. Note that participants may have mentioned privacy and security concepts throughout the interview (for example, when asked if they had any hesitations prior to device pur-chase), not just during the designated privacy and security portions. Prior to each of the designated privacy and security sections, we provided participants with a short description of each term (privacy and security) in non-technical language to focus their responses. This diﬀerentiation ultimately helped us contrast and compare participants’ perceptions of each concept as well as where they conflated the two.

Data analysis started with coding, which involves categorization of data. In the case of interview data, units of text are labeled based on their topic, with these labels being called “codes.” Units may consist of a phrase, sentence, or multiple sentences. For example, the unit of text “the companies that have the information, you know data breaches happen. . . So that was a concern as well” was assigned the code “Data Breach Concerns.” We employed both deductive and inductive coding practices, which allowed for an emergence of themes. Deductive coding involves starting with pre-defined codes that the researchers believe will appear in the data. With inductive coding, codes emerge from the data itself. Analysis of the interview transcripts began with the development of an a priori code list based on the research questions. Using the initial code list, each of the three research team members individually coded a subset of four interviews, then met as a group to discuss code application. Related codes were grouped into higher-level categories, called axial codes. For example, the codes “Data Breach Concerns,” “Audio/video access,” and “Financial loss” were combined into an axial code called “Security Concerns.” As part of the final codebook (a list of codes to be used in analysis), all codes were “operationalized,” which involves formally defining each code to ensure understanding among all coders. Using the codebook, we then coded the remaining interviews independently, with each transcript coded by two researchers. Each pair of coders then examined and resolved diﬀer-ences in code application. Throughout the analysis phase, during regular group meetings, we discussed relationships among the codes and our interpretations.

As with any interview study, participant responses are subject to recall, self-report, and social desirability biases. In addition, the participants, who were generally highly educated professionals in a high-income metropolitan area, may not be fully representative of the overall smart home user population in the U.S. However, our study population appears to mirror smart home adopters characterized in prior industry surveys [15]. We also acknowl-edge that U.S. smart home users may have diﬀerent privacy and security attitudes from those in other countries, for example, due to political or cultural factors related to privacy expectations and tolerance. In addition, our study only captures perceptions of smart home adopters of multiple devices, so does not adequately capture those of limited adopters or non-adopters. These limitations could be addressed with replication of this study in other countries or a global quantitative survey informed by the results of our study. However, even with its limitations, the study serves as an exploratory investigation that can inform subsequent surveys of broader populations.

In this section, we report results from a subset of the interview data specific to privacy and security. Note that these results often describe participant perceptions, which may or may not reflect reality. Example quotes from participants are provided throughout. Counts of participants men-tioning specific topics are provided in some cases, not as an attempt to distill our qualitative data to quantitative measures, but rather to illustrate weight or unique cases.
3.2.6 Selling of Data and Targeted Ads

Participants with virtual assistants or smart cameras discussed the “always on” mode of these devices and how audio and video are collected and stored. A smart security camera owner said, “I know it’s always recording. So it’s recording all your conversations around it, pretty much just recording everything you do and uploading it to the cloud” (P22_A). A participant with a virtual assistant commented, “I know it records and stores every com-mand that you give it, because you can retrieve them in the app, and you can actually play the recording of you saying whatever you said” (P24_A). Participants also mentioned data collected when setting up an account, for example via companion apps on their smart phones:

Another participant spoke about payment information being collected by smart entertain-ment subscription services: “If you’re doing it through the TV itself, you’re going to have to set up an account and then put in your credit card information” (P20_A). Others were less specific about the kinds of data they thought were being collected. One participant thought that his devices were collecting “everything it sees, everything it hears, everything you input into it, all the data you provide. I think it collects all of it somewhere” (P26_A). Another talked in broad terms about information being collected from his smart entertainment devices: “I’m sure they’re collecting what you’re watching, kind of your habits. I’m sure they’re collecting a lot of stuﬀ that I don’t even know about” (P18_A).

We asked participants where they thought collected data go. Twenty-three participants thought that data are sent to the smart home manufacturer. Eight of these made specific mention of the manufacturer’s cloud or cloud service as a destination. For example, one participant said, “Devices that are collecting sensor information, all that sensor informa-tion leaves your house and is stored in a cloud service” (P11_A). Others referred to manu-facturer servers or databases: “it goes to the companies, I guess their servers, a database” (P28_A). Some participants expressed uncertainty about whether manufacturers send the data elsewhere after receiving it, as demonstrated by one participant who commented, “hope-fully they’re not selling it. We don’t know” (P28_A). Another remarked:

Thirteen participants believed that manufacturers transferred or sold smart home data to third parties, most often advertisers. One participant commented, “I’m pretty sure they’re selling that information to diﬀerent advertisers. . . because the best way to make money is through ads that are specifically targeted to exactly what the person needs” (P22_A). A user believed “companies get this data and send it over to marketing firms” (P21_U). Still others thought that the government was directly collecting smart home data (6 participants). P14_U thought that data go “to Big Brother pretty much. CIA” Another participant went into more detail:

Participants were asked how they think the data collected by smart home devices are used. Several believed that data are analyzed by manufacturers for product improvement pur-poses. From a functionality perspective, one participant commented that his smart vacuum cleaner “was sending back maps of the area that it’s cleaning and scoping out, so it can improve and build better maps” (P13_A). Another remarked, “I’m sure they’re also col-lecting information about the device, if it’s faulty or if you know maybe how quickly their customer support team reaches out to us” (P28_A). Data analysis was also viewed as a way to improve future versions of the product or inform the design of completely new products. A participant believed that, through data collection, manufacturers “study con-sumers’ habits, the behavior, so that will help them to come up with better products to solve their needs” (P36_A). An owner of a smart thermostat viewed the data as contributing to a larger eﬀort to save energy: “it definitely goes into a database where they collect and an-alyze that information which actually, I’m okay with. If it’s going to save the environment, sure” (P6_U). As also reflected in participant responses related to data destination, many of the inter-viewed smart home users thought that data are used by the manufacturer or third parties for targeted advertising. One participant said that manufacturers are “doing data mining. . . It’s not malicious I don’t think. I mean everything about it is to sell you a product, everything about the internet is to sell you a product” (P40_A). Another thought that manufacturers or third parties “take that information and potentially target emails with advertisements to you, because they know where you live, they might know what type of devices you have in your house” (P11_A). A user talked about data being sold “to agencies that do these surveys to kind of figure out what’s popular out there in the market” (P21_U). A few participants saw a use of smart home data by law enforcement agencies when needed. One remarked, “If there’s a microphone in your house and they have a warrant to collect information, they’ll use it” (P2_A). Another talked about the value of law en-forcement having access to audio logs: “For criminal cases or if something really happens that’s scary or bad, it would be really good to have a way to play that information back” (P23_A). Finally, several participants personally made use of the data to monitor what is going on in their homes. For example, one discussed how she uses data from her smart door lock to monitor entry to the home: “We have a maid that comes in on Wednesdays. We know exactly when she comes in the house, when she leaves” (P14_U). Another talked about benefits of looking at the data collected by his smart thermostat:

Interviewees were asked in what ways, if any, their device or the device manufacturer pro-vides a means to control or manage what information is collected and how it is shared. Several said that they did not think there was a way to control the information (7 partici-pants) or that they did not know (11 participants). A few mentioned specific control options. A smart home administrator who owned a number of devices answered:

In the first half of interviews, participants were asked if they had any hesitations prior to device purchase, if they had any general concerns about their smart home devices, and what other members of the household thought about the devices. Two-thirds of participants men-tioned privacy-related concerns and half acknowledged security concerns in the context of these questions. These unprompted mentions oﬀer interesting insight into whether privacy and security concerns are in the forefront of users’ minds. Participants were later explicitly asked about their privacy and security concerns. In some cases, participants were personally concerned about privacy or security but to varying degrees. Other participants mentioned concerns that were expressed by others (e.g., family members, friends, media) but not personally held. For example, one participant mentioned a disparity in privacy concerns between him and his partner: “The [virtual assistant], I didn’t have any hesitations. My fiancé did because she doesn’t like being listened to all the time” (P10_A). The most frequently mentioned concerns for both privacy and security are summarized in this section. For each category of concern, we indicate whether the concern was men-tioned only in the privacy context, only in the security context, or both. Fig. 3, 4, and 5 show the number of participants expressing each type of concern. Note that some partici-pant concerns fell into multiple categories. For example, a concern about the government eavesdropping by accessing audio collected by virtual assistants falls under both the “au-dio/video access” and “government access” categories.

The most frequently mentioned concern from both a privacy and security perspective was access to audio and video recorded within the home. Some were uneasy about manufac-turers collecting this data. For example, one smart home user talked about her husband’s concerns when he is teleworking: “My husband’s paranoid [virtual assistant] is listening to him about conversations about work” (P12_U). Others were concerned about unauthorized people gaining access to the device. A participant spoke about his wife’s hesitancy about the smart cameras in the home: “I think she’s concerned about someone hacking into the cameras and watching us” (P2_A).

Two participants expressed concern about there being recording mechanisms in the devices without their knowledge. One said, “I recall a couple of years ago, [manufacturer’s] smart TVs, I think it was, had a built-in camera that the users weren’t aware of. So having stuﬀ like that that I’m not aware of is a bit concerning” (P22_A). In some cases, participants made a conscious decision not to purchase or use devices that record audio or video because of their concerns. One participant, although owning many other smart home devices, did not own a virtual assistant, saying:

A user was concerned about potential data leaks because she was not sure about “the secu-rity around, if any, the information that’s being stored” (P21_U). Multiple participants mentioned high visibility data breaches during the interview as a point of reference. Although not directly involving smart home device manufacturers, these breaches eroded overall trust in companies’ abilities to protect consumer information. One participant talked about these breaches as he believed smart home device manufacturers may also be susceptible: “You hear people’s data has been compromised, which seems to be happening fairly frequently, where you’re signed up as part of some kind of database. It’s being hacked” (P4_A). Another expressed his lack of trust:

Several participants were concerned about national governments gaining access to smart home data, especially audio and video. This concern was discussed in the privacy con-text with respect to surveillance and the security context related to governments possibly hacking into smart home devices. Among those concerned about the U.S. government obtaining the data, one participant opined, “Just from a general big brother perspective, I think you’re naive to think that we’re not being watched and the government is overreaching” (P26_A). Others were worried about foreign government espionage. A user said, “we have so many other countries that are trying to hack into our accounts” (P12_U). Another participant was concerned about supply chain issues with smart home devices: “there’s chips in there to where even the manufacturer may not even be entirely sure that the [foreign government] is monitoring what they’re doing with the device” (P3_A).

Within the security context, participants mentioned that they were concerned about their devices being hacked by unauthorized or malicious actors, as expressed by one participant who worried that hackers would be able to “shut oﬀ, or dismantle, or mess with the system that I have in place” (P37_A). In fact, the threat of device exploitation underpinned many of the privacy and security concerns discovered in our study. For example, exploitation could lead to unauthorized individuals gaining access to audio and video feeds. Governments could hack into devices or their companion apps for surveillance purposes. Several discussed the potential ease and perceived inevitability of their smart home devices being hacked. One remarked:

Participants believed that security vulnerabilities and device hacking could also result in safety consequences since smart home devices often have the ability to make changes to the physical environment. For example, since many of the participants owned smart ther-mostats, there were concerns about hackers being able to control the heating and air in the house, which could impact the physical well-being of household members. One smart home user wondered, “what if someone hacks into our phones and. . . with the [smart ther-mostat] they try to change the temperature if we’ve already set it and they go in and they try to reconfigure it on their own?” (P12_U). Others were concerned that malfunctioning or hacked devices could allow intruders easier access to the home should smart alarm systems or security cameras be disabled. A user with a smart door lock said, “If somebody could hack our system, they could eas-ily open our front door” (P14_U). P31_A commented, “If criminals were wise enough, they’d just knock out the wireless and enter these homes.” Another participant talked about potential dangers if his smart garage door opener was exploited:

Three other security-specific concerns were revealed during the interviews. Several partic-ipants were concerned about unauthorized individuals gaining access to the Wi-Fi network and other devices on that network through smart home devices, as noted by a participant: “I use my phone for everything, and it’s connected to my Wi-Fi. My Wi-Fi’s connected to my smart home. So I’m not a hacker, but I’m sure they find ways” (P41_U). Four people were worried that access to other linked accounts, e.g., email and social media accounts, could be gained by exploiting smart home device apps, especially if pass-words were common across accounts. For example, one participant said, “Our [app] ac-count is associated with an email. So if you were to hack into it, you have my email and then from my email you can get anything else” (P30_U). Two participants mentioned a concern with devices having poor default security set-tings. One commented, “One of the areas of concern with these would be if they have default passwords out of the box that are easily looked up, easily found on the internet” (P15_A). Finally, two expressed hesitations with smart home device updates from a security per-spective. As one smart home owner said about manufacturers, “They’re able to change your stuﬀ in your house. . . So there’s some kind of access from the outside” (P26_A).

We also found examples of various levels of lack of concern, with seven participants having neither privacy nor security concerns. In 24 cases, participants did not value the information collected by smart home devices, believing they would not be a worthwhile target. For example, one participant remarked, “I feel like you’ve got people who are pretty talented with computers and can get this stuﬀ. . . I’m of the mindset, have at it. We don’t do anything cool in my house, anyways” (P8_A). We also identified evidence of privacy resignation [9] in which users believe that their data are already publicly available via other means (e.g., social media, prior data breaches, etc.), and that there is nothing they can do about it (8 participants). A participant expressed this resignation when she said, “If you don’t think people have all of your information already, you’re crazy” (P17_A). Finally, five participants viewed hacking as a nebulous concept with a low probability of occurrence, especially among those who did not think they would be interesting enough to target. For example, a participant commented, “Some people are concerned about hacking, but that seems to be kind of a remote thing that people would be interested in doing” (P3_A).

During the privacy and security portions of the interviews, participants were asked if they performed any mitigations to alleviate their concerns. Although we summarize mitigations in this paper, a more in-depth discussion of protective measures identified in the study is included in another paper [12]. Mitigations, along with examples given by participants, are shown in Table 2. We observed that all the identified mitigations were discussed at least once within both the privacy and security contexts as participants often conflated the two concepts or mitigations were viewed as being eﬀective for both. We also noticed that most mitigations mentioned in the interviews were rather simplistic, for instance, setting a device app or Wi-Fi password. We explored reasons why some participants do not take mitigative actions. Obviously, some were simply not concerned enough to put forth the eﬀort to take any action. Others were not aware of available options or were not given options. For example, one smart home user commented, “I’ve been given very little methods to alleviate the concerns. Usu-ally the description of the controls aren’t specific enough for me to alleviate my concerns” (P13_A). Another said, “I can only image what you can and can’t turn oﬀ. There’s prob-ably some things. Whether or not that actually happens or the user just thinks that it’s turned oﬀ, I don’t know” (P2_A). Some lacked the knowledge to choose eﬀective mitigations, especially within the secu-rity context. For example, P34_A commented, “I’m not really like an IT guy, or like tech savvy. . . There’s just so little I can tell about that.” Another participant said, “I know it is password protected. That’s as far as my knowledge. I don’t know more than that. I’m not certified with cybersecurity” (P41_U). Via in-depth, semi-structured interviews, we investigated users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security. Our results suggest that users often have incomplete knowledge of what smart home data are collected and how they are being used. Despite having privacy and security concerns, users often accept risks as a tradeoﬀ for perceived benefits. We also found that concerns do not always result in taking mitigative action for a number of reasons, most centered on lack of available options, transparency, or knowledge. The examination of users’ perceptions of smart home privacy and security can begin to inform possible ways in which a diverse range of users can be more empowered to take protective actions for their smart home devices and feel more comfortable when introduc-ing these devices into their homes. These might include improvements in the usability of privacy and security mechanisms or options that manufacturers could provide in their products.

We asked study participants several questions related to their perceptions of smart home data collection and usage. We summarize their responses in this section.

Participants were asked what data, if any, they thought their smart home devices were collecting. Most were aware that data were being collected but provided diﬀerent levels of specificity as to the kinds of data. Types of data mentioned during the interviews included home environment readings, energy usage, issued commands, audio, video, entertainment viewing, and account and service subscription information, among others. One participant described his perceptions of collected data:

“I’m sure that the [smart thermostat] is collecting, I know it’s collecting how hot I’m heating the room, how long it’s being heated, time periods which it’s being heated. . . The plugs, I’m sure they collect how long they’re on for, how frequently they get turned on and oﬀ, how much power it’s providing to the external outlet” (P10_A).

A technically-savvy, do-it-yourselfer created a separate segment on his home network that only contained smart home devices. He regularly monitored the traﬃc leaving the network, observing as much as possible the kinds and volume of smart home data sent out of the network even though much of it was encrypted:

“I know they are collecting environmental data. I know they are collecting certain event data, and, unfortunately, I know they’re also collecting voice data inside the premises. I also know they are collecting our energy usage profiles. . . There’s packets attempting to leave every day. Yesterday I ran a profile. There was six megabytes of data that was trying to leave the network” (P16_A).

“All these devices require an account, so you’re giving them your email and you’re probably opting in, whether you know it or not, on them sending your information to third parties. So they now have your name, in a lot of cases your address, phone number, maybe even a cell phone number, your email address, and whatever password you associate with that email address” (P11_A).

“I know for a fact, the way the [virtual assistant] and the other voice-based smart devices work is every audio segment that it records gets sent back to a server to be analyzed. And what they do with it after it’s received is a little bit of a question mark” (P15_A).

“I assume it’s compiled somewhere in a research lab of the government. . . And I can only imagine there is some like poor sap somewhere in the government who has to weed through like thousands and thousands of data. . . to maybe find something. But I assume it’s just some basement in the government” (P30_U).

Finally, several participants provided vague answers to the question about data destina-tion. Five talked about the data going out to the internet in general, e.g., “Up in internet world” (P12_U). Four others were not sure. For example, one said, “I kind of think that it goes nowhere. . . Who knows?” (P23_A). Another expressed apathy: “Who knows?. . . I guess, who cares, is my answer” (P8_A).

“If there’s something I notice in that data that’s actionable, I’ll try to take action. . . With the HVAC system, if I’m noticing that it’s running a lot more than I would like it to or expect it to or it’s not aﬀecting the temperature change as quickly as it should, then that might tip me oﬀ that it’s time to change a filter. Or maybe I want to check if any windows are cracked or if there are any leaks, any areas that I want to insulate, things like that. I mean, it has tipped me oﬀ to the furnace having problems running and starting, things like that” (P15_A).

Multiple interviewees discussed how device and manufacturer privacy policies and user level agreements are meant to provide information on data collection and use, but few found that information to be satisfactory or easily understood. One participant talked about man-ufacturers providing privacy-related information: “Sometimes I think, by law, they might have to update, or at least send out, their information on privacy, what data are collected, et cetera. . . It’s laborious, it’s in lawyer speak” (P31_A). Another commented:

“There’s the end user licensing agreement for everything that’s 100 pages long, no one ever reads. But everything is disclosed in there if you care to read it, which nobody ever does. I don’t think I’ve read one my entire life” (P40_A).
Several participants expressed a general lack of trust related to manufacturer’s reported data collection policies. For example, one smart home administrator commented:

“I don’t have much trust in what companies say they collect and don’t col-lect. I think they collect what they can and use it. Even if they say they’re not collecting it, I think it’s being used somehow” (P10_A).

Another participant reflected, “I don’t trust the information that’s provided, so I don’t really believe that when they say they’re transparent, that they really are” (P22_A). A smart home owner discussed how he believes control options for data collection are set to the advantage of manufacturers: “I feel like the default is always full access, so you have to really look for and pursue stricter settings” (P18_A).

“Depends on the device. Like the light bulbs and the plugs give you nothing. The [smart entertainment device] gives you a couple of choices between usage statistics and problem, like if there’s a failure or something. . . It gives you the choice to automatically report like a crash. But it also gives you the choice like if you just want usage statistics to be sent to [manufacturer], which I don’t. So the thermostat’s like that too, you have the choice send them extra information for their diagnostic, whatever that means, purposes” (P13_A).
Another participant spoke about settings she remembered seeing on her devices:

“They have choices where you can say send your data, or don’t send your data, or like I said the [virtual assistant] has a ‘delete your history daily,’ or store it for whatever. I forgot what the other options were, but I just automatically chose delete it daily” (P27_A).
Several participants were vaguely familiar with some data collection settings, but not sure about all options available to them. For example, one participant commented:

“I think I’ve read that [virtual assistant] has the option to delete some informa-tion. I know that there’s a physical mute button on the side of them that you can flip. . . It turns everything oﬀ. I don’t know about anything beyond that. I don’t know enough about whether or not there’s a way to control what specifically it deletes, or if I can be like, delete everything” (P29_A).

Several remarked that opting out of certain data collection practices can be diﬃcult. Two participants were aware that a letter had to be sent to the manufacturer in order to opt out, with one of those saying, “There’s an opt-out thing that no one’s ever going to do. . . I saw the address, a mailing address, and I, out of curiosity, was like, ‘What is this mailing address for?’ It was the opt-out” (P3_A). Another smart home owner was resigned to the fact that she did not have much of choice with respect to opting in or out of data collection: “at the end it’s like, okay, if I want to use this device, I have to opt in” (P17_A). P41_U was also resigned: “No one reads the agreements. We just want to use our device, so we just agree to it, I guess.”
